title-group.article-title: Production and Characterization of a Liquid Organic Fertilizer From Black Soldier Fly (Hermetia illucens) Frass, Exuviae, and Oil Palm Empty Fruit Bunches: A Circular Economy Approach

abstract.p: The increasing generation of organic waste from agricultural and agro-industrial activities highlights the need for technologies that enable nutrient recovery and support a circular bioeconomy. This study developed a liquid organic fertilizer (LOF) from black soldier fly (BSF; Hermetia illucens) frass, BSF exuviae, and oil palm empty fruit bunches (OPEFB) through aerobic fermentation. The formulations comprised dried BSF frass, dried BSF exuviae, molasses, an Effective Microorganisms 4 (EM4) bioactivator, OPEFB, and water. Two formulation–fermentation conditions were evaluated, with OPEFB loadings of 0.6 and 0.3 kg and fermentation periods of 12 and 14 days for LOF_1 and LOF_2, respectively. Each condition was prepared in a single fermentation batch, and the results were interpreted descriptively. Laboratory analyses showed pH values of 7.00 and 6.62, organic carbon contents of 9.47% and 8.15%, organic nitrogen contents of 1.80% and 2.04%, and total nitrogen contents of 2.10% and 2.45% for LOF_1 and LOF_2, respectively. The total macronutrient concentrations (N + P₂O₅ + K₂O) were 6.13% and 6.74%, respectively. No Salmonella spp. was detected, and Escherichia coli counts were below 1 × 10² colony-forming units per milliliter (CFU mL⁻¹). However, neither formulation met the Indonesian regulatory requirements for organic carbon, total macronutrient content, and Fe, while several other required parameters were not analyzed. The Material Circularity Indicator (MCI), calculated using the Ellen MacArthur Foundation methodology, was 0.918 for LOF_1 and 0.908 for LOF_2 within the defined active-material boundary. The operational electricity-related carbon footprints were 1.2523 and 1.4563 kg CO₂e batch⁻¹, respectively. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining BSF residues and OPEFB to produce a nutrient-containing liquid product with high material circularity under the specified calculation assumptions. Further formulation optimization, comprehensive quality assessment, and agronomic evaluation are required to establish its suitability for agricultural application.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: A growing population and increasing demand for food place additional pressure on agricultural production systems and the natural resources required to sustain them (Godfray et al., 2010; Kopittke et al., 2019). At the same time, the intensification of agricultural production generates considerable quantities of organic residues that require appropriate management and valorization. Consequently, resource-efficient techniques that recover nutrients and organic matter from agricultural and food-system residues are increasingly important for advancing circular agricultural systems. Population growth also drives solid waste production, leading to significant environmental problems. Poor waste management poses significant dangers to human health and has detrimental consequences on animal and marine life. In its 2024 Food Waste Index Report, the United Nations Environment Programme (2024) estimated that approximately 1.05 billion tonnes of food were discarded worldwide in 2022 by households, food-service providers, and retailers. This estimate is higher than the 931 million tonnes reported in the 2021 edition for 2019. Beyond the loss of valuable resources, inadequate management of organic waste contributes to greenhouse gas emissions, particularly methane generated under anaerobic conditions. Emissions associated with this process have been estimated to represent 8–10% of global GHG emissions (Ungureanu & Vlăduț, 2026). Such environmental pressures demonstrate the limitations of conventional linear waste-management systems and reinforce the importance of adopting circular approaches that prioritize resource recovery and waste valorization. These objectives are consistent with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 12.5 (Waste Reduction) and SDG 13 (Climate Action) (Ungureanu & Vlăduț, 2026). Integrating waste management with food security strategies is therefore important for achieving more sustainable resource-use systems (Lal et al., 2020).

Organic waste is commonly managed through landfilling, composting, and anaerobic digestion, although each method presents specific environmental or operational limitations. Land disposal can result in persistent environmental problems, including methane (CH₄) generation, leachate formation, and potential contamination of surrounding soil and groundwater (Koda et al., 2017). Composting offers a more environmentally favorable alternative in many circumstances; however, it generally requires considerable processing time and land area, and the resulting products may have limited added value. Anaerobic digestion provides an opportunity to recover energy in the form of biogas, but its implementation involves substantial capital and operating costs. Furthermore, the digestate produced may require additional treatment or appropriate disposal (Mertenat et al., 2019). These limitations have encouraged the development of alternative biological treatment technologies that can achieve waste reduction while recovering useful materials and generating higher-value products.

Biological conversion using insects has consequently gained attention as an alternative approach to organic waste management. Among the available species, the black soldier fly (BSF, Hermetia illucens L.) is particularly promising because of its ability to utilize a broad range of organic substrates, including food residues, the organic fraction of municipal solid waste (MSW), agricultural by-products, animal manure, and sewage sludge. Under favorable operating conditions, BSF larvae can reduce the volume of organic waste by approximately 50–80% (Salam et al., 2022; Ungureanu & Vlăduț, 2026). This process also generates several recoverable products, thereby supporting resource utilization within a circular bioeconomy. For example, larvae can be cultivated using different organic substrates, including manure (Fitriana et al., 2022; Gärttling & Schulz, 2022; Lamanna et al., 2026), and subsequently processed into protein-rich ingredients for pet food (Freel et al., 2021), poultry and pig feed (Barragan-Fonseca et al., 2017; da-Silva et al., 2024), and aquaculture applications (Belghit et al., 2019). Other BSF-derived materials also have potential industrial applications. Chitin-containing compounds recovered from insect residues can serve as raw materials for various bio-based products (Soetemans et al., 2020), while larval oil has been investigated for biodiesel production (Odoi-Yorke et al., 2025), bio-lubricant applications (Mukhriza et al., 2026), and cosmetic formulations (Rabani et al., 2019).

BSF larvae cultivation not only provides a protein source but can also produce residue in the form of BSF larvae frass, a mixture of remaining solid waste and exuviae (shed exoskeletons). Previous research has shown that the substrate and rearing conditions affect the dry weight of larvae produced during BSF cultivation (Schmitt & de Vries, 2020). Furthermore, previous research projected that global BSF production would increase by approximately 1 million tonnes by 2025 (Chia et al., 2019). Several factors, such as the type of organic waste and the cultivation area, determine the increase in BSF frass volume (Lopes et al., 2022). This predicted growth in frass output requires new approaches to its use and management.

BSF frass may contain nutrients and organic matter beneficial for plant growth, but its characteristics depend strongly on the feedstock and degree of stabilization. Direct application of insufficiently stabilized frass may pose risks associated with ammonia and other phytotoxic compounds (Alattar et al., 2016). Therefore, the nutrient composition, pH, organic carbon, and microbiological safety of a frass-based LOF must be characterized before agricultural application.

The chemical characteristics of BSF frass are closely associated with the substrates consumed by the larvae. According to Lopes et al. (2022), total carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) concentrations are relatively consistent across different feeding substrates, averaging approximately 37% and 3%, respectively. By comparison, phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) exhibit greater variation, with reported concentrations of 1–5% and 0.5–4.1%, respectively. Micronutrient concentrations are also influenced by feed composition, whereas pH (approximately 7.5) and the C/N ratio (approximately 15) appear comparatively stable. The influence of dietary composition is further illustrated by individual feeding experiments. Setti et al. (2019) used the Gainesville House Fly diet and obtained frass containing 44 g kg⁻¹ N, 52 g kg⁻¹ P, and 44 g kg⁻¹ K. In another experiment, Klammsteiner et al. (2020) compared chicken feed, grass residues, and fruit and vegetable waste as separate larval substrates. The resulting frass contained between 18.3 g kg⁻¹ N (fruit and vegetable waste) and 25.9 g kg⁻¹ N (chicken feed). Similarly, Lopes et al. (2020) demonstrated that modifying the dietary composition could alter the nitrogen content of BSF frass. When larvae were raised on bread waste, the resulting frass contained 15.2 g kg⁻¹ N; incorporating 5–15% fish waste increased this concentration to 18.4–23.8 g kg⁻¹ N. These findings indicate that the nutritional characteristics of BSF frass can be influenced by adjusting the composition of the larval feed.

The agronomic performance of BSF frass is influenced by both application rate and crop characteristics. Excessive application may have adverse effects because ammonia released during nitrogen mineralization can cause phytotoxicity (Green & Popa, 2012). This potential risk was observed in maize, where high frass application rates were associated with reduced plant height and leaf production (Alattar et al., 2016). However, positive crop responses have also been reported when frass is incorporated into balanced fertilization strategies. For example, applying composted BSF frass together with nitrogen–phosphorus–potassium (NPK) fertilizer resulted in higher yields of French beans (Phaseolus vulgaris L.), tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum L.), and kale (Brassica oleracea L. var. acephala) than using NPK fertilizer alone (Anyega et al., 2021).

Previous studies have reported beneficial effects of liquid organic fertilizers (LOFs) derived from various organic materials on vegetable production. BSF-derived frass and exuviae have also been investigated as agricultural amendments, suggesting their potential for nutrient recycling in agriculture. The concepts of sustainable agriculture and the circular bioeconomy emphasize the recovery and reuse of organic residues in agricultural production systems. The palm oil industry generates substantial quantities of oil palm empty fruit bunches (OPEFB), a residue containing lignocellulose, organic carbon, and minerals. OPEFB can be used as a soil amendment, compost feedstock, a feedstock for biochar production, or a substrate for beneficial bacteria. However, its utilization remains limited; it is commonly used as mulch or disposed of in open areas, potentially contributing to environmental contamination (Bharudin et al., 2022).

Despite the potential of these materials, the combined use of BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB as feedstocks for LOF production remains underexplored. In particular, the physicochemical properties, nutrient composition, and microbiological safety of LOF produced from this combination of secondary biomass materials have not been adequately characterized. In addition, the material circularity of such a formulation, particularly within a defined active-material boundary, has received limited attention. Therefore, this study aimed to produce an LOF from BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB and to characterize the resulting product in terms of its physicochemical properties, nutrient composition, microbiological safety, and material circularity.

sec.title: 2.1. Materials and liquid organic fertilizer preparation
sec.p: This laboratory-based experimental study investigated the use of BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB waste in the production of LOF. BSF frass was obtained from larvae reared on chicken manure. Two formulations were prepared to produce LOF. The equipment and materials used in the experiment are listed in Table 1. The quantities listed in Table 1 represent the available stock of raw materials, whereas the actual quantities used in each LOF treatment are provided in Table 2.

caption.title: Materials and equipment available for the experiment
Formulation and fermentation conditions of the two LOF treatments

sec.p: The two LOF treatments represented different combinations of formulation and fermentation conditions rather than independent tests of individual process parameters. LOF_1 contained 600 g of OPEFB and was fermented for 12 days, whereas LOF_2 contained 300 g of OPEFB and was fermented for 14 days. Because OPEFB loading and fermentation time varied simultaneously, their individual effects cannot be separated. Therefore, differences between LOF_1 and LOF_2 are interpreted as differences between the two overall treatment conditions rather than as the effects of either factor alone.

Figure 1 shows the aerobic fermentation process used to produce LOF. BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB were sun-dried, ground using a chopper, and sieved to obtain a uniform particle size. Molasses was diluted and mixed with Effective Microorganisms 4 (EM4). All materials were then placed in an aquarium containing 10 L of water, and an aerator with two outlets supplied air to the mixture. Fermentation was carried out for 12 days for LOF_1 and 14 days for LOF_2, with manual stirring every 2 h. After fermentation, the mixture was filtered to separate the LOF from the solid residue.

caption.title: The process of making LOF using frass and BSF exuviae

sec.p: During fermentation, total dissolved solids (TDS), electrical conductivity (EC), and liquid temperature were measured using a Sojipro 4-in-1 water quality meter. The aroma and color of the mixture were assessed through sensory and visual observations, respectively, as qualitative indicators of fermentation progress. These parameters were used to monitor the process but were not used to evaluate the final product quality.

The quality of the LOF was evaluated against the minimum technical requirements for LOF specified in Decree No. 261/KPTS/SR.310/M/4/2019 (Ministry of Agriculture of the Republic of Indonesia, 2019). Physicochemical, nutrient, and microbiological analyses were conducted by an external analytical laboratory. The results for LOF_1 and LOF_2 were compared descriptively.

sec.title: 2.2. Experimental design and replication
sec.p: The experiment comprised two LOF treatments, LOF_1 and LOF_2, which were prepared under different formulation and fermentation conditions (Table 2). Each treatment was produced in a single fermentation batch (n = 1 per treatment). One sample from each batch was submitted for laboratory analysis, and the laboratory reported results for 12 parameters per sample. These results represent analyses of one sample per treatment rather than independent fermentation replicates. Accordingly, no inferential statistical tests, including analysis of variance (ANOVA), were performed, and the results are presented descriptively.

Water served as the process medium and carrier. Because the assessment focused on the active biomass-derived materials and additives, water was excluded from the MCI calculation. The active-material input comprised molasses, EM4, BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB. The total active-material input (M) was 2.8155 kg for LOF_1 and 2.5155 kg for LOF_2. Both formulations contained 0.5155 kg of virgin materials (molasses and EM4), whereas the secondary materials amounted to 2.30 kg in LOF_1 and 2.00 kg in LOF_2. This system boundary was defined a priori and applied to both the LFI and MCI calculations. Therefore, the reported MCI values describe circularity on an active-material basis rather than on the basis of the total product mass, including water.
The MCI was then calculated as:

where, F(X) is the utility factor and X represents the utility of the product. The utility factor accounts for differences in product lifetime and intensity of use relative to the industry average (Ellen MacArthur Foundation & Granta Design, 2015). Because no industry-average utility data were available for LOF, the product was assumed to have average utility (X = 1). Under this assumption, F(X) = 0.9, and Eq. (2) simplifies to MCI = 1 − 0.9 × LFI.

MCI values range from 0 to 1, with values closer to 1 indicating higher material circularity. For interpretation, MCI scores were classified into four categories, as presented in Table 3. Molasses and EM4 were weighed before mixing. The measured masses were 0.3625 kg for 250 mL of molasses and 0.153 kg for 150 mL of EM4, yielding a total virgin-material mass (V) of 0.5155 kg per batch.

The operational carbon footprint was estimated for one LOF production batch, which served as the functional unit. Each batch was prepared using 10 L of water as the initial liquid input. The final LOF volume after fermentation and filtration was not measured; therefore, the results are expressed per batch rather than per liter. The system boundary included electricity consumption by the chopper during material preparation and by the aerator during aerobic fermentation. Upstream feedstock production, transportation, laboratory analyses, water supply, and downstream application were excluded. The carbon footprint (CF, kg CO₂e batch⁻¹) was calculated as:

where, Pi is the rated power of equipment i (watt), ti is its operating time (h), and EF is the grid emission factor (kg CO₂e kWh⁻¹). The aerator had a rated power of 5 watts and operated continuously for 288 h for LOF_1 and 336 h for LOF_2. The chopper had a rated power of 400 watts and operated for 5 min (0.083 h) per batch. A grid emission factor of 0.85 kg CO₂e kWh⁻¹ was adopted from Decree No. 163.K/HK.02/MEM.S/2021 (Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources of the Republic of Indonesia​​, 2021).

sec.title: 3. Result
sec.p: The LOF quality was evaluated on the basis of macronutrients (N, P₂O₅, and K₂O), organic carbon, micronutrients (Fe, Mn, and Mo), pH, and microbiological safety (Escherichia coli and Salmonella). The nutrient composition of BSF frass depends strongly on the larval feeding substrate and on the decomposition process (Gärttling & Schulz, 2022). Organic nitrogen (organic-N) refers to the fraction of nitrogen bound to organic compounds, and higher values indicate a larger pool of slow-release nitrogen. Both LOFs exceeded the minimum organic-N requirement of 0.5% (Table 4). These values fall within the upper quartile of reported BSF frass values (Beesigamukama et al., 2020) and are higher than the organic-N content reported for household-waste LOF (below 1%) (Haryanta et al., 2022). The pH values of 7.00 (LOF_1) and 6.62 (LOF_2) were within the required range. The organic-C contents were 9.47% (LOF_1) and 8.15% (LOF_2). Both values are below the minimum requirement of 10%, so neither LOF met the organic-C criterion.

The total-N contents were 2.10% (LOF_1) and 2.45% (LOF_2), respectively, indicating their potential as nutrient sources. LOF_2, which contained 300 g OPEFB and was fermented for 14 days, had a higher nitrogen content than LOF_1, which contained 600 g OPEFB and was fermented for 12 days. However, because OPEFB loading and fermentation duration varied simultaneously, this difference cannot be attributed independently to either factor. Agronomic effectiveness requires further validation through replicated plant-growth experiments.

The combined N + P₂O₅ + K₂O contents were 6.13% (LOF_1) and 6.74% (LOF_2). Both values exceed the upper limit of 6%, so neither LOF meets the macronutrient criterion. Diluting the product would lower the macronutrient content but would also reduce organic-C further below 10%. The formulation itself, not only the water content, therefore needs adjustment. These results do not indicate a high-quality fertilizer; they describe the nutrient concentrations of the tested batches only.

The Fe concentrations were 960 ppm (LOF_1) and 1,204 ppm (LOF_2), and both exceed the maximum limit of 900 ppm. Fe is an essential micronutrient for chlorophyll formation. However, Fe concentrations above the regulatory limit indicate non-compliance and may cause Fe toxicity in sensitive crops, especially in acidic or waterlogged soils. The high Fe levels probably came from the OPEFB feedstock or from contact with metal equipment during processing; the source was not determined. These Fe concentrations are also above the typical range reported for BSF frass (Beesigamukama et al., 2020; Haryanta et al., 2022). The Mn concentrations (280 and 265 ppm) and Mo concentrations (6 and 2 ppm) were within the required ranges, although the Mo content of LOF_2 was at the lower limit. E. coli counts were below 1 × 10² colony-forming units per milliliter (CFU mL⁻¹), and Salmonella was not detected in either LOF.

Overall, both LOFs met the requirements for organic-N, total-N, pH, Mn, and Mo but did not meet those for organic-C, P₂O₅, total macronutrient content, and Fe. In addition, several parameters required by the decree, including heavy metals and the micronutrients Zn, Cu, and B, were not analyzed. The microbiological results showed no detectable Salmonella and E. coli counts below the laboratory-reported threshold; however, direct comparison with the regulatory microbiological limit is restricted by the different reporting units. Consequently, neither product can be considered fully compliant with Decree No. 261/KPTS/SR.310/M/4/2019 (Ministry of Agriculture of the Republic of Indonesia, 2019). Further formulation adjustments and comprehensive quality analyses are required before the products can be registered or recommended as liquid organic fertilizers.

Because each formulation was prepared as a single fermentation batch (n = 1), no inferential statistical tests were performed, and the results were interpreted descriptively. The 12 laboratory parameters for each LOF represent analytical results from one sample per batch rather than independent biological replicates. During fermentation, TDS ranged from 3299 to 8195 ppm, EC from 12.43 to 16.27 µS/cm, and the temperature from 25.7 to 27.2 °C.

BSF frass has been investigated as a feedstock for both solid and liquid fertilizers, including formulations combined with BSF exuviae and other additives (Kagehi et al., 2025; Yeow et al., 2026). Its combined application with mineral NPK fertilizers has also been studied in vegetable production (Anyega et al., 2021). BSF frass and BSF exuviae are abundant by-products of Hermetia illucens rearing, whereas OPEFB is an abundant by-product of the oil palm industry. These materials are not yet fully utilized. Their availability may provide a feedstock base for future scale-up. Using these by-products as raw materials follows the circular-economy principle of converting waste into resources. Their economic feasibility, however, was not assessed in this study. The material flow and circularity results are presented in Table 5.

caption.title: Material flow and MCI values of LOF_1 and LOF_2

sec.p: The LOF production system followed a waste-to-resource approach and used BSF frass (1.4 kg), BSF exuviae (0.3 kg), and OPEFB (0.6 kg in LOF_1 and 0.3 kg in LOF_2) as secondary materials. In LOF_1, secondary materials made up 81.7% of the 2.8155 kg active-material input, and virgin materials (molasses and EM4) made up 18.3%. In LOF_2, the corresponding shares were 79.5% and 20.5%. Water was excluded from the MCI calculation because it acted as a process medium and carrier.

With V = 0.5155 kg and W = 0, the LFI was 0.0915 for LOF_1 and 0.1025 for LOF_2. With F(X) = 0.9, the MCI was 0.9176 for LOF_1 and 0.9078 for LOF_2 (Table 5). Both values fall in the “very circular” category in Table 3. The lower MCI of LOF_2 reflects its smaller OPEFB input, which raised the virgin-material share. These values depend on the assumptions W = 0 and X = 1 and on the exclusion of water.

Electricity use and the operational carbon footprint were calculated based on the actual fermentation duration each treatment (Eq. (3)). The energy consumption and operational carbon footprint results for both treatments are summarized in Table 6. For LOF_1, the aerator, rated at 5 watts, operated continuously for 12 days (288 h) and consumed 1.4400 kWh. The chopper, rated at 400 watts, operated for 5 min and consumed 0.0333 kWh. Total electricity use was 1.4733 kWh, corresponding to an operational carbon footprint of 1.2523 kg CO₂e batch⁻¹. For LOF_2, the aerator operated for 14 days (336 h) and consumed 1.6800 kWh. Including the chopper’s electricity consumption, total electricity use was 1.7133 kWh, corresponding to 1.4563 kg CO₂e batch⁻¹. The higher footprint of LOF_2 resulted from its longer fermentation period and corresponding aeration time. Because the final LOF volume was not measured, the footprint is reported per batch only.

sec.title: 4.1. Circular valorization of black soldier fly residues and oil palm empty fruit bunches for liquid organic fertilizer production
sec.p: Aerobic fermentation can convert organic residues into a liquid product containing soluble nutrient fractions. Previous studies have demonstrated that BSF-derived residues contain variable amounts of nutrients and organic matter, with their characteristics influenced by the feedstock and subsequent stabilization or post-treatment processes. Therefore, the physicochemical characteristics of LOF produced from BSF residues should be interpreted in relation to both the initial feedstock composition and the processing conditions.

The use of BSF frass in fertilizer production has expanded beyond its direct application, with previous studies exploring its incorporation into liquid formulations, microbial biofertilizers, and combined nutrient-management systems (Anyega et al., 2021; Kagehi et al., 2025; Yeow et al., 2026). These studies highlight the potential of BSF frass to be combined with other biomass-derived materials and nutrient sources to develop different fertilizer products. Building on this research, the present study incorporated OPEFB together with BSF frass and BSF exuviae to produce LOF through aerobic fermentation, extending the use of BSF-derived residues to include an additional agricultural biomass resource.

This approach contrasts with traditional organic fertilizer production, which typically relies on composting or direct application of solid waste to the land (Sari, 2022). The present method converts BSF biomass into a nutrient-containing liquid product with potential applications in foliar spraying or fertigation. The use of BSF frass and BSF exuviae as feedstocks also represents a form of biomass cascade utilization, in which residues generated from one biological production process are redirected to another value-generating application. This concept aligns with broader approaches to cascade processing and organic-waste biorefineries (Agnihotri et al., 2025). However, the present study did not quantify the release or transformation of individual soluble compounds during fermentation; therefore, such mechanisms should be considered as a conceptual interpretation rather than a directly measured process outcome.

This composition indicates that most of the resources used were derived from biomass streams previously categorized as waste. The use of frass from BSF bioconversion is a concrete implementation of a circular economy because it can convert organic waste into value-added products while returning nutrients to the agricultural system (Lopes et al., 2022). In addition to providing macronutrients and micronutrients, frass may contain chitin, microorganisms, and other bioactive components, although these components were not independently characterized in the present study.

Compared with conventional organic fertilizer production systems, which generally rely on primary raw materials, this system represents a potential circular nutrient-management pathway, as post-production solid residues can be reused as compost, BSF cultivation media, or soil conditioners. Although the MCI value is close to one, scientific interpretation must be approached with caution, as this indicator is calculated based on the mass of active materials, excluding water as a carrier. This approach is more representative for LOFs, as water does not function as a primary nutrient component. The use of an active-material basis also aligns with the principle of circularity evaluation for biomass-based products, which emphasizes the retention of functional materials over the total mass of the product.

From an environmental perspective, the operational carbon footprint was calculated from electricity consumption during material preparation and aerobic fermentation. The operational electricity demand was dominated by aeration, indicating that fermentation duration is an important operational consideration in the energy performance of the process. The absence of heating or pressurized processing further limits the electricity demand within the defined system boundary. Future optimization should therefore consider aerator efficiency, aeration control, and renewable electricity supply. The aerator was the dominant electricity-consuming equipment, accounting for approximately 97.7% and 98.1% of electricity consumption in LOF_1 and LOF_2, respectively, whereas the chopper accounted for the remainder. The higher operational carbon footprint of LOF_2 was associated with its longer aeration period within the respective formulation–fermentation condition. Furthermore, the use of BSF frass and OPEFB as secondary raw materials may provide an alternative pathway for biomass valorization; however, avoided emissions from conventional waste management and reductions in synthetic fertilizer use were not quantified in this study. Various studies have reported that integrating BSF into organic waste management can reduce greenhouse gas emissions while increasing resource recovery efficiency compared with conventional composting systems. When the indicators are considered together, the results describe a production system with a high share of secondary-material input and measurable electricity-related emissions within the defined system boundary. The MCI characterizes material circularity on an active-material basis, whereas the carbon-footprint calculation represents operational electricity-related emissions rather than a full life-cycle environmental assessment. Therefore, the present results provide an initial sustainability characterization rather than evidence that the LOF has a lower overall environmental impact than conventional fertilizer systems. Future work should apply a comparative life-cycle assessment to quantify avoided emissions and environmental trade-offs. Previous studies have demonstrated that the physicochemical and microbiological features of BSF-derived wastes vary depending on the feedstock and subsequent processing conditions (Basri et al., 2022). BSF frass contains plant nutrients and microorganisms and may also be a source of bioactive compounds; however, its composition varies with the feedstock, and its effects on soil and plant metabolism remain incompletely understood (Lopes et al., 2022). Previous studies have also indicated that the stabilization of BSF frass involves the decomposition and transformation of organic matter, which can promote nutrient mineralization and influence nutrient availability for plant uptake (Lopes et al., 2022). However, microbial activity and changes in nutrient solubility during the aerobic fermentation process used in the present study were not directly measured. Therefore, these mechanisms should be regarded as literature-supported possibilities rather than demonstrated effects of the present process.

Recent field research has shown that BSF frass compost can improve soil fertility and crop productivity under field conditions (Zaato et al., 2025). BSF frass consists of residual organic matter, microbial metabolites, and bioactive substances that can encourage beneficial rhizosphere microorganisms and improve nutrient cycling. Comprehensive assessments indicate that BSF frass can improve fertilizer use efficiency, reduce nutrient losses, and support circular agriculture by recycling nutrients originally contained in organic waste (Zaato et al., 2025). In the context of liquid fertilizer production, this finding is particularly interesting because fermentation can convert part of the nutrient pool into a soluble form, thereby increasing the agronomic efficiency of the final product.

The use of BSF frass and BSF exuviae as raw materials may improve the functionality of the proposed liquid fertilizer. BSF exuviae contain chitinous structural materials that may contribute to the functional characteristics of BSF-derived amendments. However, chitin degradation, nitrogen-release pathways, and changes in plant–microbial interactions were not measured in the present study. Therefore, these mechanisms should be considered literature-supported possibilities rather than demonstrated effects of the present fermentation process. Furthermore, fermentation can alter the composition of organic compounds and volatile profiles in liquid fertilizers. Studies of anaerobically fermented liquid fertilizers have reported that unpleasant odors may disappear after the products become stabilized, with volatile esters potentially contributing to more agreeable odors (López-Rubio et al., 2025). However, the present study did not characterize volatile compounds or evaluate product stability during storage. Therefore, improvements in product consistency, odor, and storage stability require further investigation before their effects on agricultural suitability can be established.

A key limitation of the present experimental design is that OPEFB loading and fermentation duration varied simultaneously between LOF_1 and LOF_2. Therefore, the observed differences in physicochemical characteristics cannot be attributed to OPEFB loading or fermentation duration independently. The results should instead be interpreted as a comparison between two formulation-fermentation conditions. A factorial experimental design that independently varies OPEFB loading and fermentation duration would be required to quantify their main effects and interaction.

The primary statistical drawback of this study is the absence of independent biological replication. Each LOF formulation was developed in a separate fermentation batch. Although several observations were collected during the experimental process and laboratory analyses, they originated from the same batch and therefore cannot be considered separate biological replicates. Accordingly, the present results describe the characteristics of the tested batches rather than population-level treatment effects.

From a circular bioeconomy perspective, the production of LOF from BSF frass represents a substantial improvement over conventional residue management. Existing BSF production systems generally focus on extracting insect biomass for animal feed, while BSF frass and BSF exuviae are often underutilized or applied with minimal processing. As a result, the enormous value of these resources remains unrealized. Reviews of the BSF-based circular bioeconomy consistently emphasize that maximizing the utilization of processing residues is crucial for improving the environmental and economic performance of insect biorefineries.

sec.title: 4.2. Liquid organic fertilizer as an implementation of the circular economy and its potential contributions to the sustainable development goals
sec.p: The utilization of BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB as LOF feedstocks is consistent with the circular-economy principle of retaining biomass resources in productive use. Previous studies have highlighted the potential of organic and agricultural residues to serve as feedstocks for value-added biobased products (Adetunji et al., 2023; Mawthoh et al., 2026). In the present study, this principle is reflected in the use of secondary biomass materials as the dominant fraction of the active-material input.

The production of LOF from BSF frass and BSF exuviae offers a concrete implementation of the circular economy concept in organic waste management and sustainable agricultural systems. In typical agricultural systems, organic waste often ends up in landfills or decomposes without effective resource recovery, leading to nutrient loss and greenhouse gas emissions, particularly methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) (Yasmin et al., 2022). In contrast, bioconversion technology using BSF can convert organic waste into value-added products, including larval biomass for feed, frass as a source of organic matter and nutrients, and BSF exuviae, which are rich in chitin and minerals (Lopes et al., 2022; Ungureanu & Vlăduț, 2026). The use of BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB as raw materials for LOF extends the biomass utilization cycle through a “waste-to-value” approach (Adetunji et al., 2023; Magro et al., 2024), transforming residues previously considered waste into valuable inputs for the agricultural industry (Aït-Kaddour et al., 2024; Mawthoh et al., 2026). This strategy is in line with the principles of a circular economy, which emphasize resource recovery, efficient use of materials, and waste minimization (Velenturf & Purnell, 2021).

The laboratory results showed that the LOF contained measurable macronutrients (N, P₂O₅, and K₂O), organic carbon, and the micronutrients Fe, Mn, and Mo (Table 4), although organic-C, total macronutrients, and Fe did not meet the regulatory requirements. These nutrients have established roles in plant nutrition and physiological processes (Liu et al., 2024; Massa et al., 2025). In addition to providing nutrients, BSF frass and BSF exuviae may contain chitin and other bioactive components that have been investigated for their potential effects on soil microbial activity, soil health, plant–soil interactions, and plant tolerance to biotic stressors (Anedo et al., 2025; Lopes et al., 2022). The measured nutrient composition indicates potential for use as an organic fertilizer; however, plant uptake, crop yield, long-term soil effects, biological soil-conditioning effects, nutrient-use efficiency, and reductions in synthetic fertilizer use were not evaluated in the present study. These potential applications may support the transition to regenerative agricultural systems that emphasize maintaining soil fertility, enhancing microbial biodiversity, and sustaining on-farm production (Kumar et al., 2025).

The research results show that LOF produced from BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB represents a potential circular nutrient-management pathway through resource recovery within the defined material boundary. This is reflected in the MCI values of 0.9176 (LOF_1) and 0.9078 (LOF_2) (Table 5), both of which fall within the “very circular” category according to Table 3. These values characterize material circularity within the specified active-material boundary and calculation assumptions, rather than the overall environmental sustainability or agronomic performance of the products.

Previous reviews have described BSF frass as a potential organic fertilizer and summarized its nutrient composition, biostimulant compounds, microbial profiles, and potential effects on plant growth and environmental sustainability (Abd Manan et al., 2024; Lopes et al., 2022). These reviews also highlight the influence of feedstock composition and production conditions on the properties of BSF frass, as well as its potential role in maintaining soil fertility and supporting nutrient recycling. BSF bioconversion also generates value-added products, including larval biomass, oil, and frass, providing opportunities to retain material value within the bioeconomy (Lopes et al., 2022). Nevertheless, the agronomic benefits and environmental improvements reported in these studies were not directly evaluated in the present study.

Previous experimental studies have reported that BSF-based bioconversion can reduce organic waste volume by 37–79%, depending on the feedstock, while reductions of 65–85% have been reported for kitchen waste under optimized conditions (Arshad et al., 2023; Magee et al., 2021). Mass-balance studies have also demonstrated nutrient recovery through conversion into larval biomass, with nitrogen bioconversion efficiencies reaching 38% (Parodi et al., 2020). Furthermore, comparative assessments have reported substantially lower direct greenhouse gas emissions from BSF-based waste treatment than from conventional open-windrow composting (Mertenat et al., 2019). These findings demonstrate the resource-recovery potential of BSF bioconversion systems. Although these findings highlight the broader resource-recovery potential of BSF bioconversion, the present study focused on LOF production and characterization and did not quantify waste-volume reduction, nutrient recovery efficiency, or avoided greenhouse gas emissions.

The production of LOF from BSF residues is potentially relevant to several SDGs. This technology may contribute to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) by providing organic fertilizer with potential applications in sustainable agricultural production (Hiywotu, 2025), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) by providing an alternative route for organic waste valorization and potentially reducing pollution risks associated with unmanaged waste disposal (Abubakar et al., 2022), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) by implementing circular-economy principles and resource reuse (Khajuria et al., 2025), SDG 13 (Climate Action) through the potential reduction of emissions associated with organic waste management and the possible substitution of conventional inorganic fertilizers (Tamasiga et al., 2025), and SDG 15 (Life on Land) through potential benefits for soil quality and biodiversity (Bach et al., 2020). In the present study, the findings are most directly relevant to SDG 12 through the recovery and reuse of secondary biomass materials and to SDG 13 through the assessment of electricity-related carbon emissions within the defined operational boundary. However, the carbon-footprint assessment does not demonstrate net greenhouse gas emission reductions because no comparative life-cycle assessment or avoided-emission analysis was conducted. Potential contributions to SDG 2, SDG 6, and SDG 15, particularly those related to crop productivity, water pollution, soil quality, and biodiversity, depend on subsequent agricultural applications and environmental performance, which were not directly evaluated in the present study. Therefore, combining BSF technology with LOF production may contribute to a circular nutrient-management system that integrates waste management, nutrient recovery, environmental conservation, and sustainable agriculture. This approach positions residues from BSF bioconversion as potential resources for supporting a more resilient, low-emission, and resource-efficient food system (Ungureanu & Vlăduț, 2026). Further agronomic and environmental assessments are required to establish its broader contributions to sustainable development.

sec.title: 5. Conclusion
sec.p: This study revealed that LOF made from a combination of BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and empty oil palm fruit bunches has the potential to serve as a value-added, circular-economy-based organic fertilizer that supports sustainable agriculture. Laboratory analysis showed organic-N contents of 1.80% and 2.04% for LOF_1 and LOF_2, respectively, while total-N contents were 2.10% and 2.45%, respectively. However, neither LOF met the requirements of Decree No. 261/KPTS/SR.310/M/4/2019 for organic-C (below 10%) and Fe (above 900 ppm), while the total macronutrient concentrations exceeded the maximum permitted limit of 6%. Several required parameters were also not analyzed. In addition, microbiological test results showed that Salmonella was not detected and that E. coli counts were below the laboratory-reported threshold (1 × 10² CFU mL⁻¹). The two formulation–fermentation conditions produced different physicochemical characteristics. LOF_2 showed a higher combined macronutrient concentration than LOF_1, whereas LOF_1 showed a higher pH and organic carbon. Because OPEFB loading and fermentation duration were varied simultaneously and each formulation was prepared in a single fermentation batch, these differences cannot be attributed independently to either factor and should be interpreted as descriptive characteristics of the tested conditions. The integration of BSF frass, BSF exuviae, and OPEFB provides a potential circular nutrient-management pathway by converting secondary biomass materials into LOF. The MCI values of 0.9176 for LOF_1 and 0.9078 for LOF_2 represent high circularity scores within the defined active-material boundary and under the specified calculation assumptions; they do not directly measure post-production material recovery. The operational electricity-related carbon footprints were 1.2523 and 1.4563 kg CO₂e batch⁻¹ for LOF_1 and LOF_2, respectively. After further formulation adjustments and comprehensive quality assessment, the LOF may be developed into an organic fertilizer for horticultural cultivation, while also providing an alternative route for biomass-waste valorization consistent with the principles of waste-to-value and the circular economy. Its potential contributions to sustainable development goals require further agronomic and environmental validation.
